specAnchors.text: know that many reactions are readily reversible and that they can reach a state of dynamic equilibrium in which: i the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction ii the concentrations of the reactants and the products remain constant

primer.text: Some reactions run both ways at once, and the two opposing half arrows say so. This note reaches dynamic equilibrium: forward and backward rates tied, concentrations constant yet unequal, and the whole balancing act demanding a closed system whenever gases would otherwise slip away.

modules.title: Reversible reactions and the two-way arrow
modules.opening: Some reactions refuse to finish: the products themselves re-form the reactants. The two half-arrows of the reversible equation announce a chemistry that runs in both directions at once, the seedbed of every equilibrium idea.
keyPoints: Reactions going to completion stop when reactants are fully used up.
Reversible reactions run backward too: their products rebuild the original reactants.
The reversible arrow (two opposing half arrows) marks a reaction running both ways.
Both the forward and the backward reaction occur simultaneously once products appear.

low.restatement: Completion reactions empty the reactant jar; reversible reactions keep refilling it from the products, so both directions run in the same vessel.
low.analogy: A leaky bucket that also refills from its own overflow: the water level settles somewhere in between, never empty, never full.
low.examPointer: Always use the equilibrium half-arrows in equations once reversibility is claimed - a single arrow wrongly implies completion.

medium.restatement: Reversibility means the product molecules retain the ability to regenerate reactants; the forward rate starts high and falls, the backward rate starts at zero and rises, and they converge at equilibrium.
medium.analogy: Two escalators running in opposite directions with shifting passenger flows that eventually balance.
medium.examPointer: Label forward and backward rates on sketches; equilibrium is where they cross, not where the concentrations are equal.

modules.title: Dynamic equilibrium and the closed system
modules.opening: Equilibrium is motion in balance: forward and backward rates equal, concentrations constant - but not equal to each other. And the balance needs walls: gases reach equilibrium only in closed systems, though solution reactions manage even in open flasks.
keyPoints: In dynamic equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal in a closed system, and concentrations stay constant.
Equilibrium concentrations are constant, not equal - the common misconception the examiners love.
A closed system loses neither reactants nor products; an open system can lose matter and energy.
Gas equilibria need closed vessels; solution reactions in open flasks lose negligible material by evaporation.

low.restatement: At equilibrium both reactions still run at identical rates, freezing the composition in place; the freezing requires a closed vessel when gases would otherwise escape.
low.analogy: A conveyer belt feeding a leak-proof warehouse at exactly the rate stock leaves the shelves: levels steady, movement never ceasing.
low.examPointer: Write 'constant, not equal' when describing equilibrium concentrations - the exact misconception examiners set as distractors.

medium.restatement: Dynamic equilibrium is a kinetic steady state: two opposing rates cancel in effect. Closure matters because escaping matter cannot be replaced by the backward reaction; open flasks still work for solutions where evaporation is negligible.
medium.analogy: Two identical pumps pushing water around a sealed loop keep levels fixed; unplug the loop and the levels drift.
medium.examPointer: Quote the hydrogen iodide example (2HI <=> H2 + I2) when asked to illustrate a dynamic equilibrium.

glossary.definition: A reaction whose products rebuild the original reactants, written with two opposing half arrows.
The state in a closed system where forward and backward rates are equal and concentrations remain constant.
A setup from which no reactant or product can escape the reaction mixture.
A setup losing matter or energy to the surroundings, which prevents gas equilibria.
